verses.zh: 耶和华晓谕摩西说：
verses.en: [NOTE:1] The Lord spoke to Moses,
notes: The account recorded in this chapter is one of the best known events in all of Scripture. In the argument of the book it marks the division between the bondage in Egypt and the establishment of the people as a nation. Here is the deliverance from Egypt. The chapter divides simply in two, vv. 1-14 giving the instructions, and vv. 15-31 reporting the victory. See among others, G. Coats, “History and Theology in the Sea Tradition,” ST 29 (1975): 53-62); A. J. Ehlen, “Deliverance at the Sea: Diversity and Unity in a Biblical Theme,” CTM 44 (1973): 168-91; J. B. Scott, “God’s Saving Acts,” The Presbyterian Journal 38 (1979): 12-14; W. Wifall, “The Sea of Reeds as Sheol,” ZAW 92 (1980): 325-32.

verses.zh: 「你吩咐以色列人转回，安营在比・哈希录前，密夺和海的中间，对着巴力・洗分，靠近海边安营。
verses.en: “Tell the Israelites that they must turn and camp[NOTE:1] before Pi Hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea; you are to camp by the sea before Baal Zephon opposite it.[NOTE:2]
notes: The two imperfects follow the imperative and therefore express purpose. The point in the verses is that Yahweh was giving the orders for the direction of the march and the encampment by the sea.

The places have been tentatively identified. W. C. Kaiser summarizes the suggestions that Pi Hahiroth, as an Egyptian word, may mean “temple of the [Syrian god] Hrt” or “The Hir waters of the canal” or “The Dwelling of Hator” (“Exodus,” EBC 2:387; see the literature on these names, including C. DeWit, The Date and Route of the Exodus, 17).
verses.commentary:
14:2 "Tell" This is a Piel IMPERATIVE (BDB 180, KB 210). YHWH is in full control.

- He hardened Pharaoh's heart, Exod. 14:4,8,17

- He delivered them, Exod. 14:13

- He fought for them, Exod. 14:14,25

- He (His angel) separated the Egyptian army and the Israelites all night, Exod. 14:20

- He split the Red Sea (by His staff in Moses' hand), Exod. 14:21

- He threw the Egyptian army into confusion (as He did the Canaanite armies in the conquest), Exod. 14:24

- He caused their chariots to swerve (VERB'S meaning uncertain), Exod. 14:25

- He closed the split in the Red Sea so as to destroy the entire Egyptian force that pursued, Exod. 14:27-28

Notice how Israel responded, Exod. 14:31!

▣ "turn back and camp" These are two commands (Qal IMPERFECT used in a
JUSSIVE retrace their route. To the Egyptians it looked like aimless wanderings and that the Israelites
were trapped by the water.

▣ "Pi-hahiroth" F. B. Huey, A Study Guide Commentary, Exodus, p. 63, suggests the name is Egyptian
and could mean

- "region of salt marshes"

- "house of the goddess Hathor"

The Hebrew root (BDB 809, cf. Num. 33:7) means "a place of meadows." The location of the site is uncertain.

There has been speculation that the phrase means "mouth of the diggings," and refers to a manmade
channel which was dug during this period (i.e., 1290 B.C. by Seti I) passing near Qantara (cf. IVP Bible
Background Commentary, p. 90).

▣ "Migdol" This (BDB 154) means "watch tower." There were many cities by this name. Its location, as
most others in this context, is uncertain. Many current Bible study maps have been influenced by which of
the three theories of the route of the exodus their producers hold: northern, central, or southern.

▣ "Baal-zephon" This (BDB 128) means "Lord of the north" (cf. Ps. 48:2; Isa. 14:13). This shows
that Canaanite fertility worship (i.e. Ba'al) had spread to Egypt.

This location is either

- in the delta region west of the Nile River

- on a peninsula of the Mediterranean on the highway to Canaan called "the way of the Philistines." See
The MacMillan Bible.

Also, map #48. Many of the exact locations of this name are uncertain.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY
WORSHIP OF THE ANCIENT NEAR EAST

▣ "by the sea" The Israelites were trapped between the sea, the desert, and the Egyptian army. This
body of water could be the Mediterranean (northern route), the Bitter Lakes (middle route), or the Red Sea (southern route).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE ROUTE
OF THE EXODUS (uncertain)

verses.zh: 法老必说：『以色列人在地中绕迷了，旷野把他们困住了。』
verses.en: Pharaoh will think[NOTE:1] regarding the Israelites, ‘They are wandering around confused[NOTE:2] in the land—the desert has closed in on them.’[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “and Pharaoh will say.”

The word translated “wandering around confused” indicates that Pharaoh thought the Israelites would be so perplexed and confused that they would not know which way to turn in order to escape—and they would never dream of crossing the sea (S. R. Driver, Exodus, 115).
The expression has also been translated “the desert has shut [the way] for them,” and more freely “[the Israelites are] hemmed in by the desert.”
verses.commentary:
14:3

NASB, NRSV
"wandering aimlessly"

NKJV
"bewildered"

TEV
"wandering around"

NJB
"wandering to and fro"

JPSOA
"astray in the land"

REB
"in difficult country"

LXX
"wandering in the land"

Peshitta
"strangers in the land"

This VERB (BDB 100, KB 115, Niphal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE)
is a rare word found only three times in the OT.

- Exod. 14:3 ‒ of people

- Esther 3:15 ‒ of people

- Joel 1:18 ‒ of cattle

The basic idea is "in confusion."

verses.zh: 我要使法老的心刚硬，他要追赶他们，我便在法老和他全军身上得荣耀；埃及人就知道我是耶和华。」于是以色列人这样行了。
verses.en: I will harden[NOTE:1] Pharaoh’s heart, and he will chase after them. I will gain honor[NOTE:2] because of Pharaoh and because of all his army, and the Egyptians will know[NOTE:3] that I am the Lord.” So this is what they did.[NOTE:4]
notes: In this place the verb חָזַק (hazaq) is used; it indicates that God would make Pharaoh’s will strong or firm.

The form is וְאִכָּבְדָה (veʾikkavedah), the Niphal cohortative. Coming after the perfect tenses with vav (ו) consecutives expressing the future, this cohortative indicates the purpose of the hardening and chasing. Yahweh intended to gain glory by this final and great victory over the strength of Pharaoh. There is irony in this expression since a different form of the word was used frequently to describe Pharaoh’s hard heart. So judgment will not only destroy the wicked—it will reveal the glory and majesty of the sovereignty of God.
This is the perfect tense with the vav (ו) consecutive. But it announces the fulfillment of a long standing purpose—that they might know.
Heb “and they did so.”
verses.commentary:
14:4 "I will harden Pharaoh's heart" This emphasizes that God is sovereign. Several times in Exodus
it says that God hardened Pharaoh's heart and several times it says that Pharaoh hardened his own heart (see
note at Exod. 4:21). The exact relationship between the two is uncertain. Nevertheless, it is obvious that
God used Pharaoh to accomplish His will and yet he was still responsible! This is similar to Judas Iscariot.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PREDESTINATION

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD HARDENED

▣ "he will chase after them" This is the fulfillment of Exod. 4:21. YHWH is in control of time, space, history.

▣ "I will be honored" This (BDB 457, cf. Exod. 14:17-18) is the Hebrew word, kabod, "glory."

SPECIAL TOPIC: GLORY (kabod, OT)

▣ "and all his army" The military force that Pharaoh had immediate access to was his royal guard. This
was 600 chariots mentioned in Exod. 14:7,23, not the full Egyptian army which would have been spread throughout the Egyptian forts.

▣ "the Egyptians will know that I am the Lord" The plagues lasted about
eighteen months and each one of them was an embarrassment to an Egyptian deity. YHWH was working with the Egyptians'
faith (cf. Exod. 9:20-21; 10:7) as He was with the Hebrews' faith (cf. Exod. 14:18; 7:5,17).

SPECIAL TOPIC: KNOW

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL
REDEMPTIVE PLAN

verses.zh: 有人告诉埃及王说：「百姓逃跑。」法老和他的臣仆就向百姓变心，说：「我们容以色列人去，不再服事我们，这做的是甚么事呢？」
verses.en: When it was reported[NOTE:1] to the king of Egypt that the people had fled,[NOTE:2] the heart of Pharaoh and his servants was turned against the people, and the king and his servants said,[NOTE:3] “What in the world have we done?[NOTE:4] For we have released the people of Israel[NOTE:5] from serving us!”
notes: Heb “and it was told.” The present translation uses “reported,” since this involves information given to a superior.
The verb must be given a past perfect translation because the fleeing occurred before the telling.
Heb “and they said.” The referent (the king and his servants) is supplied for clarity.
The question literally is “What is this we have done?” The demonstrative pronoun is used as an enclitic particle for emphasis (R. J. Williams, Hebrew Syntax, 24, §118).
Heb “released Israel.” By metonymy the name of the nation is used collectively for the people who constitute it (the Israelites).
verses.commentary: 14:5 "What is this we have done" The Hebrew slaves' freedom made a drastic economic and social disruption to Egyptian culture.

verses.zh: 法老就预备他的车辆，带领军兵同去，
verses.en: Then he prepared[NOTE:1] his chariots and took his army[NOTE:2] with him.
notes: Heb “bound.”
Heb “his people.”
verses.commentary:
14:6 "chariot" This instrument of war was developed by the Hittites of Asia Minor. They used a two or
three-man chariot. At this time Egypt used their chariots for mobility only.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARIOTS

verses.zh: 并带着六百辆特选的车和埃及所有的车，每辆都有车兵长。
verses.en: He took 600 select[NOTE:1] chariots, and all the rest of the chariots of Egypt,[NOTE:2] and officers[NOTE:3] on all of them.
notes: The passive participle of the verb “to choose” means that these were “choice” or superb chariots.
Heb “every chariot of Egypt.” After the mention of the best chariots, the meaning of this description is “all the other chariots.”

The word שָׁלִשִׁם (shalishim) means “officers” or some special kind of military personnel. At one time it was taken to mean a “three man chariot,” but the pictures of Egyptian chariots only show two in a chariot. It may mean officers near the king, “men of the third rank” (B. Jacob, Exodus, 394). So the chariots and the crew represented the elite. See the old view by A. E. Cowley that linked it to a Hittite word (“A Hittite Word in Hebrew,” JTS 21 [1920]: 326), and the more recent work by P. C. Craigie connecting it to Egyptian “commander” (“An Egyptian Expression in the Song of the Sea: Exodus XV.4, ” VT 20 [1970]: 85).
verses.commentary:
14:7 "select chariots" This (BDB 103, KB 119, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE) means that these
were the best or newest chariots and soldiers. They made up an elite royal force garrisoned at the delta capital. They were
Pharaoh's royal bodyguard.

▣ "officers" This term (BDB 1026 III) may refer to the second or third man in each chariot. Pictures of
Egyptian chariots had only two occupants (see Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, p. 122).

- one to drive

- one to shield

- one to do combat

verses.zh: 耶和华使埃及王法老的心刚硬，他就追赶以色列人，因为以色列人是昂然无惧地出埃及。
verses.en: But the Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and he chased after the Israelites. Now the Israelites were going out defiantly.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “with a high hand”; the expression means “defiantly,” “boldly,” or “with confidence.” The phrase is usually used for arrogant sin and pride, the defiant fist, as it were. The image of the high hand can also mean the hand raised to deliver a blow (Job 38:15). So the narrative here builds tension between these two resolute forces.
verses.commentary:
14:8

NASB, NRSV
"boldly"

NKJV
"with boldness"

TEV
"triumphantly"

NJB
"confidently"

JPSOA, REV, NET
"defiantly"

LXX
"with a high hand"

Peshitta
"victoriously"

The ADVERB (BDB 926, KB 1202, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE)
basically means "to be high," Here it is used of "an uplifted hand." It can refer to a geographical position, voice, or an attitude. Here,
it refers to the sense of victory the Israelis had (cf. Num. 33:3). The same form is found in Num. 15:30, translated "who sins defiantly."

verses.zh: 埃及人追赶他们，法老一切的马匹、车辆、马兵，与军兵就在海边上，靠近比・哈希录，对着巴力・洗分，在他们安营的地方追上了。
verses.en: The Egyptians chased after them, and all the horses and chariots of Pharaoh and his horsemen and his army overtook them camping by the sea, beside Pi Hahiroth, before Baal Zephon.
verses.commentary:
14:9 "chased after them" This VERB (BDB 922, KB 1191, Qal IMPERFECT
with waw) is a hunting term or military term for an active pursuit (cf. Gen. 31:25).

verses.zh: 法老临近的时候，以色列人举目看见埃及人赶来，就甚惧怕，向耶和华哀求。
verses.en: When[NOTE:1] Pharaoh got closer,[NOTE:2] the Israelites looked up,[NOTE:3] and there were the Egyptians marching after them,[NOTE:4] and they were terrified.[NOTE:5] The Israelites cried out to the Lord,[NOTE:6]
notes: The disjunctive vav introduces a circumstantial clause here.
Heb “drew near.”
Heb “lifted up their eyes,” an expression that indicates an intentional and careful looking—they looked up and fixed their sights on the distance.

The construction uses הִנֵּה (hinneh) with the participle, traditionally rendered “and behold, the Egyptians were marching after them.” The deictic particle calls attention in a dramatic way to what was being seen. It captures the surprise and the sudden realization of the people.
The verb “feared” is intensified by the adverb מְאֹד (meʾod): “they feared greatly” or “were terrified.” In one look their defiant boldness seems to have evaporated.

Their cry to the Lord was proper and necessary. But their words to Moses were a rebuke and disloyal, showing a lack of faith and understanding. Their arrogance failed them in the crisis because it was built on the arm of flesh. Moses would have to get used to this murmuring, but here he takes it in stride and gives them the proper instructions. They had cried to the Lord, and now the Lord would deliver.
verses.commentary:
14:10 "they became very frightened" In their fear they attacked

- God's love

- God's protection

- Moses' leadership (cf. Exod. 14:11-12)

This is exactly what YHWH predicted in Exod. 13:17.

verses.zh: 他们对摩西说：「难道在埃及没有坟地，你把我们带来死在旷野吗？你为甚么这样待我们，将我们从埃及领出来呢？
verses.en: and they said to Moses, “Is it because there are no graves in Egypt that you have taken us away to die in the desert?[NOTE:1] What in the world[NOTE:2] have you done to us by bringing[NOTE:3] us out of Egypt?
notes: B. Jacob (Exodus, 396-97) notes how the speech is overly dramatic and came from a people given to using such exaggerations (Num 16:14), even using a double negative. The challenge to Moses brings a double irony. To die in the desert would be without proper burial, but in Egypt there were graves—it was a land of tombs and graves! Gesenius notes that two negatives in the sentence do not nullify each other but make the sentence all the more emphatic: “Is it because there were no graves…?” (GKC 483 §152.y).
The demonstrative pronoun has the enclitic use again, giving a special emphasis to the question (R. J. Williams, Hebrew Syntax, 24, §118).
The Hebrew term לְהוֹצִּיאָנוּ (lehotsiʾanu) is the Hiphil infinitive construct with a suffix, “to bring us out.” It is used epexegetically here, explaining the previous question.
verses.commentary:
14:11-12 This is the first of many complaints from "the mixed multitude" that came out of Egypt (mostly
in Exodus 15-17 and Numbers 14-17). They were not yet the covenant people, just a rag-tag bunch!

- some unfaithful, cf. Exod. 15:25; 16:2; 17:2-3,7; Num. 20:3,13; Ezekiel 16; Hos. 2:16

- some faithful, cf. Jer. 2:2; Hos. 2:14-15,20

- some Israelites, some mixed marriage partners, and some new Egyptian believers

verses.zh: 我们在埃及岂没有对你说过，不要搅扰我们，容我们服事埃及人吗？因为服事埃及人比死在旷野还好。」
verses.en: Isn’t this what we told you[NOTE:1] in Egypt, ‘Leave us alone so that we can serve the Egyptians,[NOTE:2] because it is better for us to serve[NOTE:3] the Egyptians than to die in the desert!’”[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “Is not this the word that we spoke to you.”

U. Cassuto (Exodus, 164) explains this statement by the people as follows: “The question appears surprising at first, for we have not read previously that such words were spoken to Moses. Nor is the purport of the protest of the Israelite foremen (v 21 [5:21]) identical with that of the words uttered now. However, from a psychological standpoint the matter can be easily explained. In the hour of peril the children of Israel remember that remonstrance, and now it seems to them that it was of a sharper character and flowed from their foresight, and that the present situation justifies it, for death awaits them at this moment in the desert.” This declaration that “we told you so,” born of fright, need not have been strictly accurate or logical.
Heb “better for us to serve.”

Since Hebrew does not use quotation marks to indicate the boundaries of quotations, there is uncertainty about whether the Israelites’ statement in Egypt includes the end of v. 12 or consists solely of “leave us alone so that we can serve the Egyptians.” In either case, the command to Moses to leave them alone rested on the assumption, spoken or unspoken, that serving Egypt would be less risky than what Moses was proposing. Now with the Egyptian army on the horizon, the Israelites are sure that their worst predictions are about to take place.

verses.zh: 摩西对百姓说：「不要惧怕，只管站住！看耶和华今天向你们所要施行的救恩。因为，你们今天所看见的埃及人必永远不再看见了。
verses.en: Moses said to the people, “Do not fear![NOTE:1] Stand firm[NOTE:2] and see[NOTE:3] the salvation[NOTE:4] of the Lord that he will provide[NOTE:5] for you today; for the Egyptians that you see today you will never, ever see again.[NOTE:6]
notes: The use of אַל (ʾal) with the jussive has the force of “stop fearing.” It is a more immediate negative command than לֹא (loʾ) with the imperfect (as in the Decalogue).
The force of this verb in the Hitpael is “to station oneself” or “stand firm” without fleeing.
The form is an imperative with a vav (ו). It could also be rendered “stand firm and you will see” meaning the result, or “stand firm that you may see” meaning the purpose.
Or “victory” (NAB) or “deliverance” (NIV, NRSV).
Heb “do,” i.e., perform or accomplish.

The construction uses a verbal hendiadys consisting of a Hiphil imperfect (“you will not add”) and a Qal infinitive construct with a suffix (“to see them”)—“you will no longer see them.” Then the clause adds “again, for ever.”sn U. Cassuto (Exodus, 164) notes that the antithetical parallelism between seeing salvation and seeing the Egyptians, as well as the threefold repetition of the word “see” cannot be accidental; so too the alliteration of the last three words beginning with ʿayin (ע).
verses.commentary:
14:13 There are more commands in this verse by Moses to the people.

- do not fear ‒ BDB 431, KB 432, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense

- stand by ‒ BDB 426, KB 427, Hithpael IMPERATIVE

- see the salvation of the Lord ‒ BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal IMPERATIVE;
the VERB "see" is repeated three times in this verse.

- see YHWH's salvation

- never see the Egyptian soldiers again!

- same as b.

▣ "salvation" This OT term (BDB 447) means "physical deliverance." It is from the root "to be spacious"
(cf. James 5:15).

The Lord is called "Savior" several times in Isaiah (cf. Isa. 19:20; 43:3,11; 45:15,21; 49:26,60; 60:16;
63:8). This is carried over into the NT (cf. Luke 1:47; 1 Tim. 1:1; 2:3; 4:10; Titus 1:3; 2:10-11; 3:4; Jude v. 25). What a great title
and a great God!

SPECIAL TOPIC: SALVATION (OT)

▣ "forever" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam).

verses.zh: 耶和华必为你们争战；你们只管静默，不要作声。」
verses.en: The Lord[NOTE:1] will fight for you, and you can be still.”[NOTE:2]
notes: The word order places emphasis on “the Lord” (Heb “Yahweh”).

The imperfect tense needs to be interpreted in contrast to all that Yahweh will be doing. It may be given a potential imperfect nuance (as here), or it may be obligatory to follow the command to stand firm: “you must be still.”
verses.commentary: 14:14 This is the essence of "Holy War." YHWH acts; Israel watches (cf. Exod. 15:3; Deut. 1:30; 3:22; 20:4).

verses.zh: 耶和华对摩西说：「你为甚么向我哀求呢？你吩咐以色列人往前走。
verses.en: The Lord said to Moses, “Why do you cry out to me? Tell the Israelites to move on.[NOTE:1]
notes: The text literally says, “speak to the Israelites that they may journey.” The intent of the line, using the imperative with the subordinate jussive or imperfect expressing purpose is that the speaking is the command to move.
verses.commentary:
14:15 "Why are you crying out to Me" There is a time to pray and a time to act! At some appropriate point,
faith must become action.

14:15-16 There are several commands from YHWH to Moses for the people.

- tell, Exod. 14:15 ‒ BDB 180, KB 210, Piel IMPERATIVE

- go forward, Exod. 14:15 ‒ BDB 652, KB 704, Qal IMPERFECT used in a
JUSSIVE sense

- lift up your staff, Exod. 14:16 ‒ BDB 926, KB 1202, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

- stretch out your hand, Exod. 14:16 ‒ BDB 639, KB 692, Qal IMPERATIVE. This is often associated
with the plagues (cf. Exod. 6:6; 7:5,19; 8:5,6,16,17; 9:22,23; 10:12,13,21,22).

- divide it, Exod. 14:16 ‒ BDB 131, KB 149, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Exod. 14:21; Neh. 9:11;
Ps. 78:13; Isa. 63:12

- go through the midst of the sea, Exod. 14:16 ‒ BDB 97, KB 112, Qal IMPERFECT used in a
JUSSIVE sense

The staff represented YHWH's power but Moses had to use it (Exod. 14:21). God chose to use human
instrumentality (cf. Exod. 3:7-10)!

verses.zh: 你举手向海伸杖，把水分开。以色列人要下海中走干地。
verses.en: And as for you,[NOTE:1] lift up your staff and extend your hand toward the sea and divide it, so that[NOTE:2] the Israelites may go through the middle of the sea on dry ground.
notes: The conjunction plus pronoun (“and you”) is emphatic—“and as for you”—before the imperative “lift up.” In contrast, v. 17 begins with “and as for me, I….”

The imperfect (or jussive) with the vav (ו) is sequential, coming after the series of imperatives instructing Moses to divide the sea; the form then gives the purpose (or result) of the activity—“that they may go.”
verses.commentary:
14:16 "on dry land" God controls the boundaries of water (cf. Gen. 1:9-10; Nah. 1:4). Here He splits and
dries the Red Sea (cf. Exod. 14:16,27,29; 15:19; Jos. 2:10; Neh. 9:11); He split and dried the Jordan River
in the conquest (cf. Jos. 3:17; 4:18,22,23; 5:1; Ps. 66:6). He splits and dries a river for Elijah and Elisha in 2 Kgs. 2:8.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WATERS

verses.zh: 我要使埃及人的心刚硬，他们就跟着下去。我要在法老和他的全军、车辆、马兵上得荣耀。
verses.en: And as for me, I am going to harden[NOTE:1] the hearts of the Egyptians so that[NOTE:2] they will come after them, that I may be honored[NOTE:3] because[NOTE:4] of Pharaoh and his army and his chariots and his horsemen.
notes: הִנְנִי (hineni) before the participle gives it the force of a futur instans participle, meaning “I am about to harden” or “I am going to harden” their heart.

The form again is the imperfect tense with vav (ו) to express the purpose or the result of the hardening. The repetition of the verb translated “come” is interesting: Moses is to divide the sea in order that the people may cross, but God will harden the Egyptians’ hearts in order that they may follow.
For the comments on this verb see the discussion in v. 4. God would get glory by defeating Egypt.
Or “I will get glory over.”
verses.commentary: 14:17 This verse clearly shows YHWH's sovereignty. See note at Exod. 14:2.

verses.zh: 我在法老和他的车辆、马兵上得荣耀的时候，埃及人就知道我是耶和华了。」
verses.en: And the Egyptians will know[NOTE:1] that I am the Lord when I have gained my honor[NOTE:2] because of Pharaoh, his chariots, and his horsemen.”
notes: The construction is unusual in that it says, “And Egypt will know.” The verb is plural, and so “Egypt” must mean “the Egyptians.” The verb is the perfect tense with the vav consecutive, showing that this recognition or acknowledgment by Egypt will be the result or purpose of the defeat of them by God.

The form is בְּהִכָּבְדִי (behikkavedi), the Niphal infinitive construct with a preposition and a suffix. For the suffix on a Niphal, see GKC 162-63 §61.c. The word forms a temporal clause in the line.
verses.commentary: 14:18 See note at Exod. 14:4.

verses.zh: 在以色列营前行走　神的使者，转到他们后边去；云柱也从他们前边转到他们后边立住。
verses.en: The angel of God, who was going before the camp of Israel, moved and went behind them, and the pillar[NOTE:1] of cloud moved from before them and stood behind them.
notes: B. Jacob (Exodus, 400-401) makes a good case that there may have been only one pillar, one cloud; it would have been a dark cloud behind it, but in front of it, shining the way, a pillar of fire. He compares the manifestation on Sinai, when the mountain was on fire but veiled by a dark cloud (Deut 4:11; 5:22). See also Exod 13:21; Num 14:14; Deut 1:33; Neh 9:12, 19; Josh 24:7; Pss 78:14; 105:39.
verses.commentary:
14:19 "The angel of God" The angel and the pillar seem to represent one reality—the presence of God (cf.
Gen. 16:7-14; 22:15; Exod. 3:2).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE
ANGEL OF THE LORD

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE CLOUD. . .THE PILLAR

verses.zh: 在埃及营和以色列营中间有云柱，一边黑暗，一边发光，终夜两下不得相近。
verses.en: It came between the Egyptian camp and the Israelite camp; it was a dark cloud[NOTE:1] and it lit up the night so that one camp did not come near the other[NOTE:2] the whole night.[NOTE:3]
notes: The two nouns “cloud” and “darkness” form a nominal hendiadys: “and it was the cloud and the darkness” means “and it was the dark cloud.” Perhaps this is what the Egyptians saw, preventing them from observing Moses and the Israelites.
Heb “this to this”; for the use of the pronouns in this reciprocal sense of “the one to the other,” see GKC 448 §139.e, n. 3.

The LXX reads very differently at the end of this verse: “and there was darkness and blackness and the night passed.” B. S. Childs (Exodus [OTL], 218) summarizes three proposals: (1) One takes the MT as it stands and explains it along the lines of the Targum and Jewish exegesis, that there was one cloud that was dark to one group and light to the other. (2) Another tries to reconstruct a verb from the noun “darkness” or make some use of the Greek verb. (3) A third seeks a different meaning for the verb “lit,” “gave light” by comparative philology, but no consensus has been reached. Given that there is no easy solution apart from reconstructing the text, and given that the MT can be interpreted as it is, the present translation follows the MT.
verses.commentary:
14:20 "the cloud along with the darkness" Usually the pillar was light at night. Therefore, this phrase

- denotes the two aspects of the cloud (i.e., shade in daytime, fire at night)

- shows the distinction between Egypt and Israel (i.e., light to Israel, darkness to the Egyptians (Targums, Symmachus)

▣ "one did not come near the other" This cloud kept the Egyptian army from attacking and the Israelites
from surrendering. Notice YHWH again used a natural occurrence (i.e., the wind, Exod. 14:21), but with
supernatural intensity and timing. It took "all night" for the wind to dry the ground (i.e., sea bed, cf. Exod. 14:16).

Just one more thought, the obvious supernatural aspect of this event is the water piles on both sides
(Exod. 14:22,29). One side could be explained by the strong east wind (14:21), but not both sides!

Also note the eyewitness detail!

verses.zh: 摩西向海伸杖，耶和华便用大东风，使海水一夜退去，水便分开，海就成了干地。
verses.en: Moses stretched out his hand toward the sea, and the Lord drove the sea apart[NOTE:1] by a strong east wind all that night, and he made the sea into dry land, and the water was divided.
notes: Or “drove the sea back” (NIV, NCV, NRSV, TEV). The verb is simply the Hiphil of הָלַךְ (halakh, “to walk, go”). The context requires that it be interpreted along the lines of “go back, go apart.”
verses.commentary:
14:21 "Moses stretched out his. . .Lord swept the sea back by a strong east wind"
Notice the three elements mentioned: God, Moses, and the wind. God often uses natural means in supernatural ways
(i.e., the ten plagues).

▣ "east wind" "Wind" is ruah (BDB 924), which can mean "wind," "breath," "spirit." The east
wind was a hot, desert wind.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE BIBLE

verses.zh: 以色列人下海中走干地，水在他们的左右作了墙垣。
verses.en: So the Israelites went through the middle of the sea on dry ground, the water forming a wall[NOTE:1] for them on their right and on their left.
notes: The clause literally reads, “and the waters [were] for them a wall.” The word order in Hebrew is disjunctive, with the vav (ו) on the noun introducing a circumstantial clause.sn S. R. Driver (Exodus, 119), still trying to explain things with natural explanations, suggests that a northeast wind is to be thought of (an east wind would be directly in their face he says), such as a shallow ford might cooperate with an ebb tide in keeping a passage clear. He then quotes Dillmann about the “wall” of water: “A very summary poetical and hyperbolical (xv. 8) description of the occurrence, which at most can be pictured as the drying up of a shallow ford, on both sides of which the basin of the sea was much deeper, and remained filled with water.” There is no way to “water down” the text to fit natural explanations; the report clearly shows a miraculous work of God making a path through the sea—a path that had to be as wide as half a mile in order for the many people and their animals to cross between about 2:00 a.m. and 6:00 a.m. (W. C. Kaiser, Jr., “Exodus,” EBC 2:389). The text does not say that they actually only started across in the morning watch, however.

verses.zh: 埃及人追赶他们，法老一切的马匹、车辆，和马兵都跟着下到海中。
verses.en: The Egyptians chased them and followed them into the middle of the sea—all the horses of Pharaoh, his chariots, and his horsemen.
verses.commentary: 14:23 "horsemen" This refers to the two or three men in each chariot. See note at Exod. 14:7.

verses.zh: 到了晨更的时候，耶和华从云火柱中向埃及的军兵观看，使埃及的军兵混乱了；
verses.en: In the morning watch[NOTE:1] the Lord looked down[NOTE:2] on the Egyptian army[NOTE:3] through the pillar of fire and cloud, and he threw the Egyptian army[NOTE:4] into a panic.[NOTE:5]
notes: The night was divided into three watches of about four hours each, making the morning watch about 2:00-6:00 a.m. The text has this as “the watch of the morning,” the genitive qualifying which of the night watches was meant.

This particular verb, שָׁקַף (shaqaf), is a bold anthropomorphism: Yahweh looked down. But its usage is always with some demonstration of mercy or wrath. S. R. Driver (Exodus, 120) suggests that the look might be with fiery flashes to startle the Egyptians, throwing them into a panic. Ps 77:17-19 pictures torrents of rain with lightning and thunder.
Heb “camp.” The same Hebrew word is used in Exod 14:20. Unlike the English word “camp,” it can be used of a body of people at rest (encamped) or on the move.
Heb “camp.”
The verb הָמַם (hamam) means “throw into confusion.” It is used in the Bible for the panic and disarray of an army before a superior force (Josh 10:10; Judg 4:15).
verses.commentary:
14:24 "morning watch" The Israelites crossed over between 2 and 6 a.m. Notice how precise the eyewitness' testimony is.

▣ "the Lord looked down" This is anthropomorphic language (cf. Exod. 3:7-9).

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD DESCRIBED AS HUMAN

▣ "the pillar of fire and cloud" This is the only place the full title appears. Usually they are listed
separately, but often both are listed (i.e., "pillar of cloud," "pillar of fire," cf. Exod. 13:21,22; Num. 14:14; Deut. 31:15).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE CLOUD. . .THE PILLAR

▣ "into confusion" The VERB (BDB 243, KB 251, Qal IMPERFECT with
waw) is used several times of YHWH's acts of defeating Israel's enemies (cf. Exod. 15:16; 23:27; Deut. 7:23; Josh. 10:10;
Jdgs. 4:15; 1 Sam. 7:10; 2 Sam. 22:15; 2 Chr. 15:6; Ps. 18:15; 144:6). YHWH fought for them. It was His victory! This is "Holy War"
terminology (i.e., YHWH's acts on Israel's behalf all through the exodus and the conquest periods).

verses.zh: 又使他们的车轮脱落，难以行走，以致埃及人说：「我们从以色列人面前逃跑吧！因耶和华为他们攻击我们了。」
verses.en: He jammed[NOTE:1] the wheels of their chariots so that they had difficulty driving,[NOTE:2] and the Egyptians said, “Let’s flee[NOTE:3] from Israel, for the Lord fights[NOTE:4] for them against Egypt!”
notes: The word in the text is וַיָּסַר (vayyasar), which would be translated “and he turned aside” with the sense perhaps of removing the wheels. The reading in the LXX, Smr, and Syriac suggests a root אָסַר (ʾasar, “to bind”). The sense here might be “clogged—presumably by their sinking in the wet sand” (S. R. Driver, Exodus, 120).

The clause is וַיְנַהֲגֵהוּ בִּכְבֵדֻת (vayenahagehu bikhevedut). The verb means “to drive a chariot”; here in the Piel it means “cause to drive.” The suffix is collective, and so the verbal form can be translated “and caused them to drive.” The idea of the next word is “heaviness” or “hardship”; it recalls the previous uses of related words to describe Pharaoh’s heart. Here it indicates that the driving of the crippled chariots was with difficulty.

The cohortative has the hortatory use here, “Let’s flee.” Although the form is singular, the sense of it is plural and so hortatory can be used. The form is singular to agree with the singular subject, “Egypt,” which obviously means the Egyptian army. The word for “flee” is used when someone runs from fear of imminent danger and is a different word than the one used in 14:5.
The form is the Niphal participle; it is used as the predicate here, that is, the verbal use: “the Lord is fighting.” This corresponds to the announcement in v. 14.
verses.commentary:
14:25 "He caused their chariot wheels to swerve" See note on God's sovereignty shown in this chapter at Exod. 14:2.

This VERB (BDB 693, KB 747, Hiphil IMPERFECT with waw)
has several connotations.

NASB
"swerve"

NKJV
"took off"

NRSV, NJB, Peshitta
"clogged"

TEV
"get stuck"

JPSOA
"locked"

LXX
"bound together the axles"

The UBS Text Project, p. 105, suggests the MT's "removed" (ויסר)
should be emended to "bound" (ויאסר). It gives it a "B" rating (some doubt).

verses.zh: 耶和华对摩西说：「你向海伸杖，叫水仍合在埃及人并他们的车辆、马兵身上。」
verses.en: The Lord said to Moses, “Extend your hand toward the sea, so that the waters may flow back[NOTE:1] on the Egyptians, on their chariots, and on their horsemen!”
notes: The verb, “and they will return,” is here subordinated to the imperative preceding it, showing the purpose of that act.
verses.commentary: 14:26 This is the reverse of Exod. 14:16.

verses.zh: 摩西就向海伸杖，到了天一亮，海水仍旧复原。埃及人避水逃跑的时候，耶和华把他们推翻在海中，
verses.en: So Moses extended his hand toward the sea, and the sea returned to its normal state[NOTE:1] when the sun began to rise.[NOTE:2] Now the Egyptians were fleeing[NOTE:3] before it, but the Lord overthrew[NOTE:4] the Egyptians in the middle of the sea.
notes: The Hebrew term לְאֵיתָנוֹ (leʾetano) means “to its place,” or better, “to its perennial state.” The point is that the sea here had a normal level, and now when the Egyptians were in the sea on the dry ground the water would return to that level.
Heb “at the turning of the morning”; NASB, NIV, TEV, CEV “at daybreak.”
The clause begins with the disjunctive vav (ו) on the noun, signaling either a circumstantial clause or a new beginning. It could be rendered, “Although the Egyptians…Yahweh…” or “as the Egyptians….”
The verb means “shake out” or “shaking off.” It has the significance of “throw downward.” See Neh 5:13 or Job 38:13.
verses.commentary:
14:27 "overthrew" This same Hebrew root (BDB 654 II, KB 707, Piel IMPERFECT with
waw, lit. "shook off") relates to YHWH as warrior (cf. Isa. 59:17).

verses.zh: 水就回流，淹没了车辆和马兵。那些跟着以色列人下海法老的全军，连一个也没有剩下。
verses.en: The water returned and covered the chariots and the horsemen and all the army of Pharaoh that was coming after the Israelites into the sea[NOTE:1]—not so much as one of them survived![NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “that was coming after them into the sea.” The referent of “them” (the Israelites) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “not was left among them as much as one.”

verses.zh: 以色列人却在海中走干地；水在他们的左右作了墙垣。
verses.en: But the Israelites walked on dry ground in the middle of the sea, the water forming a wall for them on their right and on their left.
verses.commentary: 14:29 Pharaoh was not with his army. He was not drowned.

verses.zh: 当日，耶和华这样拯救以色列人脱离埃及人的手，以色列人看见埃及人的死尸都在海边了。
verses.en: So the Lord saved[NOTE:1] Israel on that day from the power[NOTE:2] of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead[NOTE:3] on the shore of the sea.
notes: The Hebrew term וַיּוֹשַׁע (vayyoshaʿ) is the key summation of the chapter, and this part of the book: “So Yahweh saved Israel.” This is the culmination of all the powerful works of God through these chapters.
Heb “the hand,” with “hand” being a metonymy for power.
The participle “dead” is singular, agreeing in form with “Egypt.”
verses.commentary:
14:30 "the Lord saved Israel" This is the VERB form
(BDB 446, KB 448, Hiphil IMPERFECT with waw) of the NOUN
"salvation," used in Exod. 14:13.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SALVATION (OT Term)

▣ "the Egyptians dead on the seashore" The east wind miraculously blew their bodies (which floated
in their armor) onto the shore so that Israel could take their armor and weapons (see Josephus, Antiq. 2.14.6).

verses.zh: 以色列人看见耶和华向埃及人所行的大事，就敬畏耶和华，又信服他和他的仆人摩西。
verses.en: When Israel saw[NOTE:1] the great power[NOTE:2] that the Lord had exercised[NOTE:3] over the Egyptians, they[NOTE:4] feared the Lord, and they believed in[NOTE:5] the Lord and in his servant Moses.[NOTE:6]
notes: The preterite with the vav (ו) consecutive introduces a clause that is subordinate to the main points that the verse is making.

Heb “the great hand,” with “hand” being a metonymy for work or power. The word play using “hand” contrasts the Lord’s hand/power at work on behalf of the Israelites with the hand/power of Egypt that would have killed them.
Heb “did, made.”
Heb “and the people feared.”

S. R. Driver says that the belief intended here is not simply a crediting of a testimony concerning a person or a thing, but a laying firm hold morally on a person or a thing (Exodus, 122). Others take the Hiphil sense to be declarative, and that would indicate a considering of the object of faith trustworthy or dependable, and therefore to be acted on. In this passage it does not mean that here they came to faith, but that they became convinced that he would save them in the future.tn The verb is the Hiphil preterite of אָמַן (ʾaman).

Here the title of “servant” is given to Moses. This is the highest title a mortal can have in the OT—the “servant of Yahweh.” It signifies more than a believer; it describes the individual as acting on behalf of God. For example, when Moses stretched out his hand, God used it as his own (Isa 63:12). Moses was God’s personal representative. The chapter records both a message of salvation and of judgment. Like the earlier account of deliverance at the Passover, this chapter can be a lesson on deliverance from present troubles—if God could do this for Israel, there is no trouble too great for him to overcome. The passage can also be understood as a picture (at least) of the deliverance at the final judgment on the world. But the Israelites used this account for a paradigm of the power of God: namely, God is able to deliver his people from danger because he is the sovereign Lord of creation. His people must learn to trust him, even in desperate situations; they must fear him and not the situation. God can bring any threat to an end by bringing his power to bear in judgment on the wicked.
verses.commentary:
14:31 "power" This is literally "hand," cf. Deut. 34:12.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

▣ "feared" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT).

▣ "believed" This is the root "amen," which means "to be firm." It came to be imagery for
dependability and trustworthiness. This is the OT term for "faith" (cf. Hab. 2:4; see

SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH, AND FAITHFULNESS IN THE OLD TESTAMENT ).
In the New Testament it is translated into English by three different terms: faith, trust, and believe (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: "Believe" in the NT).

▣ "His servant Moses" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: MY SERVANT.

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation
of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must
not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects. Compare your subject divisions with the five translations
above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation.
Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- Exodus 14 is a prose description of the exodus, while chapter 15 is a poetic description. Also note this same
dual literary pattern in Judges 4 and 5.

- For a good discussion of YHWH as the Divine warrior (i.e., Isa. 59:15c-20), see NIDOTTE, vol. 4, pp. 545-549.

- There are three main theories of the route of the exodus (see

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE ROUTE OF THE EXODUS (uncertain)).

- the northern marshes along the Mediterranean Sea

- the central marshes of the Bitter Lakes

- the southern route, which took them across the northern tip of the body of water called the Red Sea today
